Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{5}\,\text{d}x.$ Include the arbitrary constant of integration.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=5$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{5}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{5+1}}{5+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{6}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{6})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{6}\cdot 6{x}^{5} & = \\ {x}^{5}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Antiderivative of a Monomial

question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=17$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{17}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{17+1}}{17+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{18})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\cdot 18\,{x}^{17} & = \\ {x}^{17}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we write the integrand as a power of $x$, we have ${x}^{0}=1.$ Therefore, we can use the power rule with $n=0$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 1\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ 1+0 & = \\ 1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
